title: Idea: Collective game dev?
author: CommandProtocol
selftext:
Many of us have already had fun trying out assisted game dev as solo developers.

What if we teamed up to form a studio? Imagine bringing together folks with design, programming, art, and audio skills, people who could have collaborated before AI to build something truly impressive.  

I’m not knocking things we have created so far. I’m just curious whether a group effort like this might give us the closest thing yet to an AAA game. 

I’m not a game dev, and didn’t try this out yet. I asked my operators if they’d handle a game project for me, hypothetical. I didn’t have them execute anything because they told me I could do it alone, even with my 8 subscriptions on 4 providers. They aren’t great at working in parallel yet and even if they were, I am not an artist, or a sound score expert, or an animator, let alone any of the other core roles a studio needs. There are people here who specialize in each of those things. 

TL;DR Whether people want to hit me up and see if we can find out how to make an AAA producing AI-assisted game studio, or just talk to each other and ideate or link in the comments, I think more collaboration will accelerate this pipeline as a whole.

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body:
Generally it won't work unless you can pay people. It's a very well known thing in traditional game dev circles. Unless you have a very tight group who all care about the game and have close relationships or there's money involved it usually falls apart within a couple months tops. 

What happens is it's easy to collaborate when the project is fun and exciting, then when you hit the slog of unpleasant but necessary work people fall off of the project rapidly. The other failure mode is everyone has different ideas about what to make and it creates conflicts because someone has to "lose" for the project to move forward.

Not saying it's impossible to pull off, but there's a very strong likelihood of failure.

replies.author: CommandProtocol
replies.body:
Dang. You’re right. I didn’t think that part out. You seem very experienced, I assume you were in game dev before AI?

Thank you for the detailed answer

replies.author: TechgeekOne

replies.author: Deyachtifier
replies.body:
He's essentially right, although in the Open Source world there have been some exceptions (speaking from personal experience as a (pre-AI) developer and lead for a few FOSS projects including a game or two).  The "different ideas" thing is real - it is "herding cats" to the extreme.  Another issue I ran into is that game development projects attract people who are into computer games... which means your workforce is going to get distracted into playing that new hit game that just released last week.

The exceptions where it has actually worked has been when the project focuses on recreating an existing game, or where it is built around a singular developer that can carry through the slog when people are falling off, or (most commonly) both.

All that said, I wouldn't discourage doing it - developing a game collectively is a great way to learn a ton and make friends in the process.  Get the project into a habit of "release early, release often" and steer clear of analysis paralysis and perfection chasing.

replies.author: _Dingaloo
replies.body:
you sound like you're describing multiple people working in an identical workspace, or people letting agents have free-reign rather than giving them particular goals.

It's not the complicated and not that much different than the way it was before - this person works on the player movement mechanics, that person works on player combat, and the other person works on enemy mechanics. You use your AI to develop whatever you need in that category, they use theirs, you merge to a main branch each time you complete and stabilize a feature.

I mean it's nearly exactly the same process programmers have been using for decades. AI doesn't change any of that

comments.author: blvckhippy13
comments.body:
I really want to have a small group of people I work with but I’ve been thinking about organizational structure to avoid many of the problems already brought up:  
Short (1-2 months) development times while we have no revenue  
Unanimous decision for starting projects  
Only 1 or 2 decision makers per project facet (design, art, music etc)(obviously anyone can give opinion but whoever is working on that aspect has final say)  
Shared design doc with session logs for any work done with an llm

I feel like with a very small team of \~4 people who aren’t too egotistical would have a decent chance at success (having fun and/or making money). What do yall think?

comments.author: I_pee_in_shower
comments.body:
I’ve proposed this in passing in prior threads.

Most people that enter game development from another field have some kind of”really cool idea” which they wanna make true.

I’m not like that. I like to build tools and systems and could probably help many projects, particularly with agentic development.

All we need to start as a share of repository and Slack or something similar to communicate.

Is the idea to say let’s build this game agree on the game and then just distribute responsibilities?

Or more realistically, let’s pull resources to develop common technology and approaches so that we can all build our games better?

Another thing Ive learned as a newbie is that all of these "tools" I see for sale seem really cool, but I have no idea what they do; they advertise to newbs like me about how much easier they make game development (which I knew almost nothing about)

Claude can make whatever tools it needs as it goes and they're all kind of specific to my project. I've started asking Claude to make sure to note things it learned and document tool ideas so it's not using tokens on the same thing to balance values and stuff. Works especially well before starting a new chat, makes estimates easier and takes claudes guessing out. This is just one example
